framework: CEFR Companion Volume (Council of Europe, 2020) - levels A1-C2 and the four modes of communicative activity
note: Working bank. Every statement here is TeachEd's own wording of what each level can do with grammar, written as a stand-in so generation and checking have one source of truth. Status 'draft' means a methodologist has not signed it off; only 'approved' counts as calibrated. Replace or confirm each one against the Companion Volume before relying on it.

changelog.change: Grammar skill, all levels and modes, as drafts.
Vocabulary skill, all levels and modes, as drafts.

descriptors.text: Can recognise the most basic forms (am/is/are, the simple present, plural -s) in very short familiar sentences, with a picture or the context to help.
Can use a few memorised basic forms in single sentences about themselves; frequent basic mistakes do not stop the message getting through.
Can ask and answer simple questions with memorised patterns, relying on the other person to slow down and help.
Can pass on a single word or a very short phrase from a sign or an announcement in the same simple form.
Can tell from the verb form and the time words whether a simple everyday sentence is about now, the past or a plan.
Can use the simple past, the present continuous and going to in short linked sentences; basic mistakes still occur but the meaning is clear.
Can manage short everyday exchanges in familiar tenses and correct a slip when someone prompts them.
Can relay simple facts from a short text in simple sentences, keeping the tense of the original.
Can recognise the main forms in a clear text - perfect forms, the first conditional, common modals - and understand what each one signals.
Can use a good range of common forms (present perfect, first conditional, used to) with reasonable accuracy; less common forms cause mistakes, but the meaning stays clear.
Can keep a conversation going across several tenses and change the form when they are misunderstood.
Can summarise a short text for another person, changing tense and person correctly.
Can follow how complex forms - second and third conditionals, the passive, reported speech - change the meaning in longer texts.
Can use complex forms (conditionals, the passive, reported speech) with fairly high accuracy; the few errors that remain rarely cause misunderstanding.
Can choose between forms to show attitude and certainty in a discussion and repair slips without stopping.
Can restate the ideas of a text for others, choosing forms that keep the original degree of certainty.
Can notice fine differences of form - inversion, mixed conditionals, subtle choices of aspect - and what they imply.
Can vary complex grammar for emphasis and style, with only rare slips.
Can use grammar flexibly to hedge, soften or emphasise in a discussion.
Can paraphrase a demanding text with the forms that suit the new audience and register.
Can interpret the full range of grammatical choices, including idiomatic and stylistic ones, in any text.
Can use the whole range of grammatical resources naturally and stay accurate even when their attention is elsewhere.
Can adapt grammar at once to the tone and the changing needs of a conversation.
Can pass on a nuanced text, rebuilding its grammar for the audience while keeping every shade of meaning.
Can recognise familiar everyday words and basic phrases about themselves, family and surroundings, especially with a picture or gesture to help.
Can use a small set of memorised words and phrases to give simple personal details and name common objects.
Can ask for and give very simple information using single words and set phrases, relying on the other person to repeat and help.
Can pass on a single familiar word, number or name from a sign or a short notice.
Can understand frequent words and expressions on familiar everyday topics such as shopping, work, the local area and routines.
Can use a repertoire of basic words and expressions to describe people, places and daily routine in short sentences.
Can handle short everyday exchanges with common vocabulary, asking for a word to be repeated or explained.
Can relay the main point of a short simple text in simple words, using words from the original.
Can understand the main points of clear texts on familiar topics and work out the meaning of some unknown words from context.
Can use enough everyday and topic vocabulary to talk about work, travel and current events, going round a missing word when needed.
Can keep a conversation going on familiar topics, finding another way to say a word they cannot recall.
Can explain a simple point from a text to a friend in clear everyday words, picking out the key terms.
Can understand a wide range of vocabulary on general and some specialised topics, including common idioms, and guess unfamiliar words from context.
Can use a good range of vocabulary, including collocations and common idioms, with only occasional wrong word choices.
Can vary their wording to avoid repeating themselves and recover from a missing word without help.
Can summarise and explain a text to someone else, choosing precise words to carry its argument.
Can understand a broad lexicon including idioms, colloquialisms and subtle differences of tone and register.
Can use a broad lexicon fluently, choosing words and collocations to fit register, attitude and nuance.
Can use idiomatic expressions and shift register smoothly to suit the people and the occasion.
Can explain technical or abstract vocabulary to a non-specialist, rephrasing it accurately and naturally.
Can understand virtually all vocabulary, including rare and highly colloquial expressions and the shades of meaning between close synonyms.
Can choose exactly the right word or expression for a very fine shade of meaning, including humour and irony.
Can play with wording and use idiom and cultural reference with ease.
Can recast a demanding text in different words for another reader, keeping every shade of its meaning.
